response:
- Physical nature of the resistance: It’s geometric jamming, not adhesive drag. With the blade held flat (pitch 0), the thin leading edge drops into the grill’s deep, longitudinal gaps and bears against the vertical shoulders of the grate bars. The reaction redirects the push into a downward component, which is why the sensors show a spontaneous -0.020 m Z displacement during the “straight” probe, minimal Y travel (0.015–0.017 m), and a large contact force in Y (85–150 N). The blade spans the grill and is constrained laterally by the side guide walls, so it can’t yaw or snake to relieve the jam; the rigid blade bridges unsupported gaps and bends, which is reflected in the high structural stress and near-yield material strain (0.94).

- Why more Y force won’t fix it: Because the contact geometry turns additional Y push into larger normal forces against the gap edges and further downward wedging. That increases friction and binding instead of forward motion, so the blade stays trapped while stresses rise. In short, the limiting factor is geometric interlock and force redirection into Z and bending, not insufficient shear force in Y; pushing harder just deepens the jam and risks damage.
